06302.overview: Across the plains, forests, and river valleys of what are now Poland, Lithuania, Belarus, Ukraine, Moldova, and western Russia, Ashkenazi Jewish communities developed over centuries, especially from the late Middle Ages onward. Families lived in small market towns called shtetls and in cities such as Warsaw, Vilnius, and Odessa. Many worked as merchants, tailors, bakers, teachers, artisans, or traders linking villages to wider markets. Daily life centered on synagogues, study, Sabbath meals, holidays, and the Yiddish language. Hasidism and the Jewish Enlightenment grew strongly here. Despite discrimination, pogroms, and the Holocaust, the region profoundly shaped Jewish culture worldwide.

06303.displayName: Ashkenazi Jews in Central & Southeastern Europe
06303.primaryLocated: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Moldova, Netherlands, Poland, Serbia, Slovakia
06303.overview: Across the river valleys, plains, and market towns of Central and Southeastern Europe, Ashkenazi Jewish communities lived in regions that are now Germany, Austria, Hungary, Czech Republic, and parts of the Balkans. Medieval centers such as Prague and later Vienna and Budapest became known for scholarship, trade, and printing. Families often kept shops, worked as tailors, bakers, peddlers, teachers, or craftsmen. Daily life centered on synagogues, study houses, Sabbath meals, festivals, and Yiddish language. Times of tolerance brought prosperity, but expulsions, antisemitic laws, and the Holocaust destroyed many long-established communities.

06350.displayName: Sephardic Jews in the Eastern Mediterranean
06350.alsoLocated: Egypt, France, Italy, Libya, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain
06350.overview: Our Eastern Mediterranean Sephardic Jewish region centers on the descendants of Jews expelled from Spain and Portugal in the late 15th century, many of whom settled in parts of the Ottoman Empire, including present-day Turkey, Greece, and the Balkans. These communities preserved Judeo-Spanish (also known as Ladino), a Romance language similar to Spanish. Synagogues, schools, and other institutions developed in port cities like Thessaloniki, Istanbul, and Izmir, where Sephardic Jews played a key role in commerce and scholarship. Despite facing waves of displacement and, at times, unthinkable loss—especially during the Holocaust—many traditions remain, from religious songs and holiday foods to folk tales and proverbs passed down orally.

06351.overview: Our North African Sephardic Jewish region encompasses the descendants of Jews who settled in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya after being forced out of Spain and Portugal in the late 15th century. They joined long-established Jewish populations in the region, and both groups influenced each other in the centuries that followed. Sephardic Jews in North Africa played important roles as merchants, artisans, translators, and court advisors under various regimes. Their culture often blended Iberian Jewish tradition with North African influences to produce distinct food and music. In the 20th century, many Sephardic Jews left for countries like France and Israel but they still kept their traditions alive.

06400.overview: Finland is a land of deep forests, clear lakes, and long winter nights lit by the northern lights. For centuries, Finns lived between powerful neighbors, ruled first by Sweden and later by Russia before declaring independence in 1917. They defended that freedom during World War II and then built a modern nation known for equal education, innovative design, and trust in government. Finnish culture values sisu—a quiet, stubborn courage—seen in everything from sauna traditions to world-class technology companies. Today, Finland blends ancient folklore from the Kalevala (the national epic) with cutting-edge ideas, creating a society both rooted and forward-looking.

06500.overview: Our Sweden region emerged from glacial ice as lands of lakes and islands, mountains and plains. Though the countries were often at war, the people share a common Norse heritage that includes elements of language, religion, and art, though they eventually developed cultures of their own. Situated along the western boundary of the Baltic Sea, relative geographic isolation did not stop the Swedes from influencing culture, trade, and politics in Europe and around the globe.

06501.overview: Denmark is made up of the Jutland Peninsula and more than 400 islands between the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. Though small and mostly flat, it has long looked outward to the water. In the Viking Age, Danish sailors explored and traded across Europe. Later, Denmark became a powerful kingdom that once ruled Norway and parts of Sweden. Today about 6 million people live there, most in cities like Copenhagen. Denmark is known for its strong welfare system, free education, and high voter participation. Danish culture values equality, community, and hygge—a cozy sense of comfort shared with family and friends.

06600.overview: The earliest inhabitants of our Norway region were strong, seafaring peoples. For centuries, hunter-gatherers slowly pushed north across the Baltic Sea, probing coastal fjords and inland stretches for arable land as ice melted off the untamed region. While Norwegians, Swedes, and Danes all share a common Norse heritage, over time, Norway’s resilient coastal communities evolved into a nation known for its seamanship, technology, artistry, and mythology.

06601.overview: Iceland sits in the North Atlantic, where glaciers, volcanoes, lava fields, and hot springs shape the land. People first settled the island in the late 800s, mainly Norse farmers and sailors from Scandinavia, along with some Celtic settlers. These early Icelanders formed one of the world’s oldest parliaments, the Althing, to settle disputes and make laws. For centuries, Icelanders survived through fishing, sheep farming, and strong community ties, while preserving their stories in famous sagas. In 1944, Iceland gained full independence from Denmark and built a modern society that values education, equality, and a close connection to nature.

06701.overview: Estonia and Latvia lie along the eastern Baltic Sea, where forests, lakes, rivers, peat bogs, and low plains have long shaped daily life. For centuries, most people lived in villages, farming rye and barley, raising livestock, and fishing or trading through ports such as Tallinn and Riga. Both nations declared independence after World War I, were occupied by the Soviet Union during World War II, and regained independence in 1991. Danish, Swedish, German, and Russian rule influenced architecture, government, and commerce, while local communities preserved Estonian and Latvian languages, folklore, and song traditions. Today both countries are highly educated, urban, and digitally connected.

06702.overview: Situated on the eastern edge of the Baltic Sea, Lithuania is famous for its verdant pine and birch forests and thousands of picturesque lakes. Magnificent castles are found throughout Lithuania, dating back to when it was the largest country in Europe in the 14th century. Lithuania’s recent history is one of domination by powerful neighbors, particularly the Soviet Union, including the occupation, executions, and forced exile of thousands of Lithuanians by the Soviet Union in the 20th century. Today, Lithuania is an independent nation with a strong sense of national pride. Lithuanians are avid choral singers, with the "Dainų šventė"—or Lithuanian Song and Dance Festival—held every four years.

06801.overview: Spanning over 6.5 million square miles, our Russia region is a land of epic proportions—not only due to its vast size but also because of the impact of its history, politics, and culture on the world. Most of the population lives in Western Russia, in and around the cities of Moscow and Saint Petersburg. Large swaths of the country remain uninhabited or sparsely populated due to the inhospitable climate. Some quintessentially Russian activities include celebrating Maslyanitsa, the Russian holiday that marks the end of winter; marking special occasions with vodka accompanied by zakuski (a spread of snacks); and drinking tea from a samovar, Russia’s traditional metal tea kettle.

06808.alsoLocated: Estonia, Germany, Hungary, Lithuania, Moldova, Poland, Romania
06808.overview: Stretching across the broad plains, forests, and river valleys of the East-Central European Lowlands, Ukraine and Belarus share a landscape shaped by fertile soils and major waterways such as the Dnieper and Pripyat rivers. For centuries, these lands stood at the crossroads of powerful states, including medieval Kyivan Rus, the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, and the Russian Empire. Their peoples developed farming traditions, folk music, and distinct Slavic languages. In the 20th century, both societies endured war, famine, and Soviet rule, which transformed daily life through industrialization and expanded education. Since the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991, Ukrainians and Belarusians have continued to shape their identities while drawing on deep cultural and historical roots.

06810.alsoLocated: Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia
06810.overview: Our Western Ukraine region is a land of natural wonders, UNESCO World Heritage sites, and cities such as Lviv, Uzhhorod, and Chernivtsi. It includes the Carpathian Mountains, with their lakes and forests, and the fertile Dniester River Basin. Many people in Western Ukraine speak both Ukrainian and local dialects. Close cultural ties link the region with neighbors Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, and Moldova. The region is known for intricate handicrafts such as embroidered shirts and painted Easter eggs. Unfortunately, Russian aggression has threatened even this westernmost region of Ukraine, but the local culture remains strong.

06822.overview: The Western Carpathian Basin lies where eastern Austria and western Hungary meet along the Danube River, between the Vienna Basin and the Pannonian Plain. The region includes vineyards, wheat fields, and wetlands around Lake Neusiedl, with cities such as Vienna, Eisenstadt, Győr, and Sopron. Long shaped by the Habsburg Monarchy, the region's borders changed after World War I, when Burgenland became part of Austria. Today, highways, rail lines, and open European borders connect communities across the basin. German and Hungarian traditions blend in historic town squares, thermal baths, coffeehouses, wine festivals, folk music, schnitzel, goulash, and strudel.

06824.overview: Eastern Slovakia lies where rolling lowlands rise into the Carpathian Mountains, with forested hills, river valleys, and historic cities such as Košice and Prešov. For centuries, this region sat on important trade routes in the Kingdom of Hungary, shaping a mix of cultures and languages. Slovaks form the majority, alongside Rusyn, Roma, Hungarian, and Jewish communities, each leaving marks on local life, food, music, and architecture. Medieval towns benefited from crafts and trade, while wooden churches and stone castles reflect cultural traditions. The people later experienced Austro-Hungarian rule, world wars, communism, and the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia, or the Velvet Revolution, and later independence.

06826.alsoLocated: Czechia, Germany, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Ukraine
06826.overview: Centered on the fertile Carpathian Basin and surrounded by mountain uplands, Slovakia and Hungary share a landscape shaped by the Danube River and the Carpathian Mountains. Slavic peoples settled much of the region early on, while Magyar tribes arrived in the late 800s and founded the Kingdom of Hungary. For centuries, Slovaks lived within that kingdom alongside Hungarians and other groups. The region later became part of the Habsburg Empire and Austria-Hungary. After communist rule ended in 1989, both countries restored democracy and joined the European Union. Today, modern cities, manufacturing, tourism, and strong cultural traditions help shape daily life across the region.

06830.overview: Eastern Czechia includes much of historic Moravia and part of Czech Silesia, where the Morava River basin, fertile lowlands, and uplands stretch toward Slovakia and Poland. People built farming villages, market towns, and later industrial cities, while preserving strong regional identities shaped by dialects, food, music, and religion. The region has long been known for grain, fruit, and vineyards in the south around Mikulov and Znojmo. Historic cities such as Brno and Olomouc became centers of trade, learning, and Catholic church authority. Today eastern Czechia combines strong regional traditions with modern universities, advanced manufacturing, thriving wine regions, and lively cultural festivals.

06842.overview: Southern Poland is shaped by hills, valleys, and the Tatra Mountains along the border with Slovakia. This region has long been a crossroads of trade, culture, and conflict, leaving a mark on its people. Medieval cities like Kraków grew rich from salt mines and trade routes, becoming centers of learning and art. Over centuries, southern Poland experienced foreign rule, uprisings, and war, especially during World War II. Despite hardship, local traditions—folk music, mountain dress, strong family ties, and Catholic faith—helped communities endure and preserve a strong regional identity.

06844.overview: Lesser Poland lies where rolling hills rise toward the forested Carpathian Mountains, a landscape shaped by rivers, farms, and old market towns. For centuries, the region sat near shifting political frontiers. After the late-18th-century partitions of Poland, much of it became part of Galicia. Poles, Jews, Ukrainians, and Lemkos lived in many communities, trading, worshiping, and preserving distinct traditions. The area suffered greatly during World War II, most of its Jewish population was murdered during the Holocaust and later border changes and population transfers further decreased the population. Today, it is known for strong local customs, wooden churches, folk music, and resilience rooted in a complex past.

06846.overview: Stretching along the Baltic Sea, northern Poland is shaped by sandy beaches, busy ports, wide rivers like the Vistula, and lake-filled regions such as Warmia-Masuria. For centuries, this coast connected Poland to the wider world through trade, travel, and ideas. Cities like Gdańsk grew wealthy as part of the Hanseatic League, while nearby castles recall the rule of the Teutonic Knights. The region later fell under Prussian and German rule, was heavily damaged during World War II, and saw major population shifts afterward. Yet its people preserved strong local traditions. In the 1980s, shipyard workers here helped spark the Solidarity movement, changing Poland’s future.

06848.overview: Central and eastern Poland stretch across fertile plains, river valleys, forests, and lake regions from the Vistula River to the borders of Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine. For centuries, this area was shaped by Poles, Lithuanians, Belarusians, Jews, Tatars, and other communities living side by side. Cities such as Warsaw, Lublin, and Białystok grew as centers of trade, culture, and learning. War, occupation, and communist rule deeply affected the region, including the destruction of many Jewish communities during World War II. Today, family, faith, and local traditions remain important, while farming, industry, education, and seasonal festivals help define everyday life.

06912.overview: Northwestern Croatia and Istria combine fertile plains along the Sava River, wooded hills, vineyards, and a rocky Adriatic coast. Zagreb grew as a political and market center, while ports like Pula and Rovinj linked the region to Mediterranean trade. Romans built arenas and roads, Venetians shaped coastal towns, and Habsburg rule influenced administration and architecture. Today people work in factories, tourism, farming, fishing, and wine making. Truffles, olive oil, Catholic festivals, and café culture remain important parts of daily life.

06914.overview: Central Croatia includes fertile plains, wooded hills, river valleys, and historic towns centered on Zagreb, Karlovac, and Sisak, between the Sava, Kupa, and Drava river systems. For centuries, it stood at a crossroads of Central Europe, shaped by Habsburg rule, Ottoman frontier wars, and close ties to Hungary and Austria. Many people lived in farming villages or market towns, raising corn, wheat, and livestock while following Catholic traditions. Regional dialects, folk music, wooden chapels, and dishes such as štrukli reflect this heritage. Today, Central Croatia remains the country’s political heart, blending agriculture, industry, and urban life around Zagreb.

06916.overview: The Sava River flows across fertile plains and rolling hills that connect the western Balkans with Central Europe. For centuries, Bosniaks, Serbs, Croats, and other communities built farming villages and market towns shaped by trade, migration, and the influence of both Ottoman and Habsburg rule. Cities such as Banja Luka, Zagreb, and Slavonski Brod became important centers of government, religion, and commerce. During the 1900s, much of the region became part of Yugoslavia before conflict and its breakup in the 1990s. Today, strong family ties, local traditions, and growing economies continue to shape life across the Sava Plains.

06918.overview: The Central Balkans are a land of rugged mountains, forested hills, and river valleys that have long connected Central Europe with the eastern Mediterranean. For centuries, the region was shaped by the rivalry between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires. Serbs, Bosniaks, Montenegrins, Albanians, Croats, and other communities developed distinct identities influenced by Orthodox Christianity, Islam, and Catholicism. Farming, trade, and livestock herding supported daily life, while cities such as Belgrade and Sarajevo became important cultural centers. The wars of the 1990s brought widespread destruction and displacement. Today, the region continues rebuilding while preserving its rich cultural heritage and strong family traditions.

06919.overview: Dalmatia in Croatia has steep limestone mountains, rocky valleys, long island chains, and historic towns along the Adriatic Sea. Cities such as Split, Zadar, and Dubrovnik were important ports that connected the region to Mediterranean trade routes. Dubrovnik was once the center of the Republic of Ragusa, an independent city-state known for trade and diplomacy. On islands such as Hvar and Brač, many people lived by fishing, growing olives and grapes, and working at sea. Catholic feast days, stone churches, and klapa singing (a cappella, multipart singing style) remain important traditions. Today Dalmatia is known for tourism, ferries, seafood, and seafaring culture.

06920.overview: Bordered by Italy, Austria, Hungary, and Croatia, Slovenia stretches from the Alps to the Adriatic Sea. It is a small yet geographically diverse country renowned for its stunning mountains, lush forests, and picturesque lakes. Historically part of several empires and states, independence finally came in 1991. Slovenia shares cultural traits with Central Europe while maintaining a distinct Slavic identity. Slovenians celebrate seasonal festivals, preserve their local dialects, and enjoy dishes such as dumplings and hearty stews. The countryside remains dotted with traditional farmhouses and churches, often the center of community life. Slovenians value nature and sustainability.

06930.alsoLocated: Bulgaria, Greece, Hungary, Moldova, North Macedonia, Serbia
06930.overview: Romania’s diverse landscapes include dense forests, rolling hills, and river valleys that have long supported agricultural life. Once part of the Roman Empire, the region has absorbed layers of Slavic, Ottoman, and Hungarian influence. The Romanian language, rooted in Latin, distinguishes the country from its neighbors. Folklore plays a powerful role in cultural identity, and many villages still celebrate festivals with colorful costumes, carved wooden decorations, and music played on pan flutes and violins. Whether from Transylvania or Moldavia, many Romanian families keep strong ties to their roots through stories, customs, and rural traditions.

06940.overview: The southwestern Balkans include Albania, North Macedonia, Kosovo, Montenegro, and nearby borderlands, a region of rugged mountains, deep river valleys, large lakes, and Adriatic coastline. Long a crossroads of trade and empire, the area was shaped by ancient Illyrian, Greek, and Thracian peoples, then by Roman, Byzantine, Serbian, Venetian, and Ottoman rule. Its cultures blend Slavic, Albanian, Mediterranean, and Islamic influences. Albanian, Macedonian, Montenegrin, Serbian, Bosniak, Turkish, and Roma communities all contribute to regional life. Traditions include folk songs, circle dances such as oro and kolo, and woven textiles. Family networks are often close-knit, with grandparents central to childcare and celebrations.

06950.alsoLocated: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovia, Croatia, Czechia, Hungary, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, Slovakia, Spain, Turkey
06950.overview: The early Romani people left northern India in the 9th or 10th centuries and arrived in Europe some 400 years later. Many preserved their nomadic lifestyle, in part because of Europe’s distrust of outsiders and economic competition, since Romani men were recognized for being skilled livestock traders, metalworkers, woodworkers, and basket-weavers. Throughout the Middle Ages and into modern history, discrimination and legal persecution targeting the Romani persisted, and hundreds of thousands were killed in the Porajmos—the genocide of Romani people in Nazi concentration camps. Today, along with the Romani language, other symbols of Romani pride and identity are on the rise, including radio programs, magazines, and the adoption of the Romani flag in 1971. Please note that your ethnicity results do not prove or disprove that you belong to a particular ethnic group. Identifying with, or being a member of, an ethnic or cultural group involves much more than genetics.

06990.overview: Bulgaria stretches from the snowy Balkan Mountains to the fertile Danube Plain and the sandy Black Sea coast. Its history blends Thracian roots, Roman roads, medieval Bulgarian empires, and centuries of Ottoman rule before gaining autonomy in 1878 and full modern independence in 1908. The culture reflects Slavic language, Orthodox Christian traditions, and rich folk music with uneven rhythms, fiery horo dances, and colorful embroidery. Bulgarians celebrate Kukeri festivals, make yogurt and rose oil, and honor Cyril and Methodius for the Slavic alphabet. The population is mainly Bulgarian, with Roma, Turkish, and Pomak minorities adding regional diversity.

07001.overview: Albania, in southeastern Europe, is shaped by steep mountains, fertile valleys, and a long Adriatic and Ionian coastline. This landscape has helped form a resilient and close-knit society. Albanians value strong family ties, respect for elders, and a tradition of hospitality that treats guests with honor. A cultural principle called besa, or keeping one’s word, guides personal and social relationships. Albanian culture reflects centuries of contact with neighboring regions, visible in its music, food, and customs. Folk songs feature powerful vocals, and meals often include bread, cheese, olives, and grilled meats. Today, Albanians balance pride in their history with hopes for education, travel, and new opportunities.

07050.overview: Northern and central Greece stretch from the mountains of Macedonia and Epirus to the fertile plains of Thessaly and the hills around Athens. For thousands of years, these regions have been centers of Greek history, trade, and culture. Ancient cities, Byzantine churches, and Ottoman-era landmarks reflect a long and layered past. Thessaloniki grew into an important port and cultural center, while farming and herding supported many rural communities. Today, most people live in towns and cities, but traditional foods, music, festivals, and strong family ties remain important parts of daily life.

07051.overview: The southern mainland of Greece, including the Peloponnese, features rugged hills and fertile valleys. Olive trees dominate the scenery, anchoring the local agricultural livelihood for many generations. Towns developed around strategic sites or trade routes, connecting rural areas to nearby markets. Cultural traditions showcase a strong sense of history and regional pride. Today, tourism—especially along the coast—boosts the economy, but farming remains a key part of life. The community continues to revolve around seasonal work, local cuisine, and tightly knit communities rooted in the land.

07070.overview: Pontian Greeks trace their roots to the southern shores of the Black Sea, where Greek-speaking communities lived for nearly three thousand years. They built towns, farmed mountain valleys, fished coastal waters, and traded across the Black Sea. Over time, they developed a distinct culture known for its lyra music, energetic dances, rich folklore, and unique dialect of Greek. During the early 1900s, persecution, war, and population exchanges forced many Pontian Greeks to leave their homeland and settle in Greece and other countries. Today, Pontian communities continue to preserve their heritage through festivals, music, food, and strong family traditions.

07101.overview: Scattered across the Aegean Sea, these islands are shaped as much by wind and water as by land. Rocky terrain limits agriculture, so communities have long relied on fishing, trade, and seafaring. Villages grew around harbors, with narrow streets and homes built to withstand sun and salt air. Cultural life centers on religious festivals, shared meals, and seasonal activities tied to the sea. Today, tourism is a major economic force, bringing periodic shifts to island life. Even so, many traditions endure, and daily routines—from fishing to local gatherings—remain closely tied to the maritime environment.

07102.overview: Despite its small size, Crete feels expansive, with mountains cutting across the island and fertile plains stretching toward the coast. For generations, people here have relied on olive groves, livestock, and small-scale farming for sustenance. Settlements range from isolated villages to bustling cities like Heraklion, each reflecting layers of history. Local culture carries a strong sense of independence, evident in music, food, and social customs. Today, tourism and urban development are growing, but agriculture remains central. Across the island, daily life reflects deep ties to the land, family, and a long, distinct regional identity.

07103.overview: Along Greece’s western edge, the Ionian Islands stand out for their lush greenery and gentle landscapes. Regular rainfall supports olive trees, vineyards, and small farms that have sustained local communities for centuries. These islands were shaped by long periods of Venetian and European influence, evident in their architecture and public spaces. Music and community celebrations remain especially important here. Today, tourism and agriculture together form a key part of the economy. Despite outside connections, local life keeps a steady pace, rooted in food traditions, seasonal work, and strong community ties.

07200.overview: Our Malta region, a Mediterranean archipelago between Sicily and North Africa, comprises three inhabited islands characterized by dry, rocky terrain and sandy beaches. Over time the islands of Malta have been occupied by the Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, and more recently the Arab and Norman Empires. It was these last two that left their trace on the Maltese language, which includes elements from Arabic, Romance languages, and English. Primarily Roman Catholic, present-day Malta most closely resembles southern Europe in its religion, culture, and architecture.

07300.overview: Sardinia is the second-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily. Its craggy mountains pushed up from the ocean in the Paleozoic era more than 250 million years ago. Rome, Spain, and Italy have all left their mark on Sardinian history, but even in the face of outside influences, the island has developed and maintained a culture, language, and cuisine of its own.

07401.overview: Sicily is the largest island in the Mediterranean Sea, located between Europe and Africa. The Phoenicians, Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Normans, and Spanish all left their mark on the island's culture. Sicily’s architectural heritage ranges from Greek temples to Baroque churches. Local cuisine features fresh seafood and citrus, blending Arab and Italian influences in dishes like arancini (fried rice balls) and caponata (a vegetable dish). Golden beaches, rocky sulfur mines, rolling farmland, and Mount Etna are all part of the landscape that has helped shape a people known for their warmth, storytelling traditions, and deep connection to the land and sea.

07402.overview: Central Italy's peoples have long shown skill in making the most of available resources. More than 2,500 years ago, Etruscan farmers pioneered winemaking in Tuscany's clay hills, establishing traditions that continue to influence today’s Chianti producers. Camerino's position between the Apennine Mountains and the Adriatic Sea made it a center for banking and trade. Benedictine monks in Umbria's valleys perfected olive cultivation methods that local farmers still follow. Romans used their position on the Tiber River to control Mediterranean trade. Across the region, patterns of adaptation and innovation created communities where tradition and progress could work in tandem.

07403.overview: Southern Italy's history has been shaped by its rugged environment and foreign rule. Greeks began colonizing the region in the 8th century BC, planting olive groves that still produce oil today. Byzantine emperors controlled much of Puglia and Calabria, leaving behind painted churches and fortress towns. Norman knights built stone castles to defend the countryside. Spanish kings charged heavy taxes, and peasants got creative with simple meals from ingredients like tomatoes, garlic, and herbs. Frequent earthquakes taught people to rebuild quickly. This harsh existence shaped a culture where survival depended on family and neighbors, simplicity, and determination.

07501.overview: Northeastern Italy's prosperity comes from its productive farmland and international trade. Venice became a powerful trading center by controlling routes between Eastern markets and Europe. Venetian traders sailed to Constantinople and beyond. The Veneto region's fertile plains were ideal for growing crops, while winegrowers in the Trentino-Alto Adige region developed terraced vineyards along the steep mountainsides. The city of Trieste was Austria-Hungary's main seaport, contributing to a unique blend of Italian, Austrian, and Slavic cultures. From mountains to the sea, the geography shaped this region that has thrived on agriculture, international trade, and cultural exchange.

07502.overview: Stretching from the snowy Alps to the warm Mediterranean coast, Northwestern Italy has long been a place of innovation. The rich farmland of the Po River Valley and the busy ports along the Ligurian coast gave people the resources and reasons to make world-changing achievements. The region fostered Renaissance artists like Leonardo da Vinci, merchants who started Europe's first banks, and designers who made Milan a center of global fashion. Today, this tradition of excellence continues with world-famous Barolo wines, plus modern designers, artists, and inventors who still attract visitors and business leaders from around the world.

07601.overview: France stretches from the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea, with rolling farmland, rugged mountains like the Alps and Pyrenees, and long river valleys that have supported farming and trade for centuries. Over time, its people built powerful kingdoms, experienced revolution, and helped spread ideas about citizenship, law, and rights around the world. France was shaped by Roman rule, medieval monarchs, and the French Revolution of 1789. Today, French society reflects strong regional identities, pride in language and food, and a long tradition of art, science, and public debate.

07602.overview: Brittany reaches into the Atlantic in far northwestern France, with rocky coasts, sandy bays, river inlets, and rich farmland inland. For centuries, farmers raised dairy cattle and grew grains, while fishing fleets worked the surrounding seas. Ports such as Saint-Malo and Brest connected the region to trade and naval activity. Brittany has strong Celtic roots, shaped in part by people who migrated from Britain after Roman rule declined. Medieval duchies, stone churches, roadside calvaries, and walled towns show its long history. Today, people work in farming, fishing, tourism, shipbuilding, and services, while many keep Breton traditions through music, festivals, crêpes, and cider.

07620.overview: Belgium lies at the crossroads of Western Europe, bordered by France, Germany, and the Netherlands. Its landscape includes coastal dunes, fertile farmland, and bustling cities with centuries-old architecture. Once part of the Roman Empire, it later saw Burgundian and Spanish rule before gaining independence in 1830. Its culture blends Flemish Dutch and Walloon French traditions, expressed in Gothic cathedrals, medieval guild halls, and renowned art from Bruegel to Magritte. Belgians are known for exports like chocolate, waffles, and beer. Multilingual life in vibrant cities like Brussels, Antwerp, and Liège shapes the country’s diverse national identity.

07650.overview: Acadia is a distinct cultural landscape encompassing the coastal Maritimes and expanding into parts of the St. Lawrence River valley. Long before European arrival, this was the ancestral home of the Mi’kmaq, who formed a vital alliance with French settlers from western France. These early Acadians engineered sophisticated dike systems to reclaim fertile marshlands, creating a unique way of life tied to both land and sea. Despite the trauma of the Great Expulsion (Le Grand Dérangement) in 1755, the Acadian spirit proved unbreakable. Today, this heritage thrives through the French language, spirited fiddle music, and traditional dishes like fricot, reflecting a resilient identity that spans generations and borders.

07651.overview: French settlers built communities along the St. Lawrence River, creating economies based on farming, fishing, and the fur trade. Cities such as Quebec City and Montreal became important centers of government, business, and religion. Trade and cooperation with Indigenous peoples influenced transportation, food, and daily life. Over time, a unique French-speaking culture developed, shaped by its language, laws, and traditions. Today, most people in Quebec live in cities, especially Montreal, while smaller towns continue farming and local traditions. Modern Quebec combines a diverse economy and growing immigration with a strong commitment to preserving its French language, culture, and identity.

07701.overview: Our Netherlands region is known for its flat and low-lying geography. Less than half of the country stands over three feet above sea level, and many of its most populated areas are protected by dikes and dunes. This landscape lends itself to cycling, the preferred mode of transport of many Dutch residents, and the bicycle has become a widely-recognized symbol of the Netherlands, along with windmills, tulip fields, and wooden shoes. Dutch culture has long been characterized by an attitude of tolerance and openness, attracting persecuted religious and political minorities for centuries. Today, the Netherlands is recognized for its densely populated, modern cities such as Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and The Hague.

07750.overview: From the 18th century, German settlers migrated to the Russian Empire, establishing agricultural colonies along the Volga and Black Sea regions. Invited by imperial authorities, they introduced farming innovations, built German-language schools, and organized communities around churches. Over generations, settlers adapted to steppe environments while maintaining cultural traditions. Political upheaval in the 19th and 20th centuries prompted repression, displacement, and emigration. Today, descendants of these communities are widely dispersed, notably across North and South America. In countries like the United States, Canada, and Brazil, German-Russian heritage persists through cuisine, religious practices, and community networks, although language retention has declined.

07751.alsoLocated: Belgium, Denmark, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands
07751.overview: Northwestern Germany stretches from the North Sea coast across broad plains, rivers, and fertile farmland. For centuries, farming, fishing, and maritime trade shaped local life. Cities such as Hamburg and Bremen became powerful trading centers through the medieval Hanseatic League, linking northern Europe by sea. The Protestant Reformation and later industrial growth helped transform the region’s economy and culture. Today, busy ports, manufacturing, and international trade remain important, while rural areas continue to support agriculture. Northwestern Germany combines historic market towns, coastal traditions, and modern cities, attracting people from across Germany and around the world.

07752.alsoLocated: Belgium, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Luxembourg, Switzerland
07752.overview: Bavaria & Western Austria are shaped by the Alps, the Danube River, and forests such as the Bavarian Forest. For centuries, farming, salt mining, and trade along Alpine routes supported local communities. Cities like Munich, Salzburg, and Innsbruck became important centers of commerce, music, and learning. Catholic traditions and strong regional identities continue to influence baroque churches, village festivals, and customs such as Oktoberfest and Alpine cattle drives. Today, the region is known for advanced manufacturing, engineering, tourism, and companies like BMW. Historic castles, monasteries, and mountain villages stand alongside modern cities, blending centuries-old traditions with innovation and cultural diversity.

07753.overview: Switzerland is a landlocked Alpine nation of soaring peaks, glacial lakes, and fertile valleys, bordered by France, Germany, Italy, and Austria. Its history includes Celtic tribes, Roman rule, medieval cantons forming the Swiss Confederation in 1291, and a long tradition of neutrality. The culture blends German, French, Italian, and Romansh influences, seen in multilingual towns, cheese-making, watchmaking, and precision engineering. Swiss people value direct democracy, local autonomy, and outdoor life. Festivals, chocolate, mountain railways, and global banking centers reflect a society balancing tradition, innovation, and stunning natural landscapes.

07754.overview: Northeastern Germany stretches from the Baltic Sea coast to broad plains dotted with lakes, forests, and farmland. For centuries, this region was shaped by the kingdoms of Prussia and later by German unification, with cities such as Berlin becoming centers of government, culture, and learning. Farming, trade, and military service played important roles in daily life. After World War II, the area became part of East Germany, and reunification in 1990 brought major economic and social changes. Today, Berlin is a thriving global city, while many smaller towns balance historic traditions with new opportunities and the challenges of population decline.

07755.overview: Western Czechia includes forested border mountains, river valleys, and fertile lowlands stretching across the western half of the Czech Republic. Rivers such as the Vltava River, Elbe River, and Ohře helped support farming, trade, and growing towns. Cities like Prague and Plzeň became important centers of politics, culture, and brewing. For centuries, much of this area belonged to the Kingdom of Bohemia and later the Habsburg monarchy. Religious conflict during the Reformation, followed by nineteenth-century industrial growth, also shaped the region. Today western Czechia blends historic cities, manufacturing, famous beer traditions, and strong regional identity.

07800.overview: Basque history has long been shrouded in mystery. The Basque country lies on the Bay of Biscay and in the western Pyrenees Mountains, with four provinces in Spain and three in France. The Basques have been living there longer than anyone can remember. Their language is probably the oldest in modern Europe and appears to be unrelated to any other known language in the world. Despite being an ancient people, the Basques currently have no nation of their own. They’re defined by being Basque—not by borders.

07901.overview: Our Northern Spain region includes Galicia, Asturias, Cantabria, and a portion of Castile-León. Bordered to the north by the Bay of Biscay and interwoven with heavily forested mountain ranges, this segment of the Iberian Peninsula is known for fiercely resisting outside rule from a long list of invaders, including Romans and Moors. For over 1,000 years, Christian pilgrims have flocked to the rumored tomb of Saint James at Santiago de Compostela, while others have entered prehistoric caves in the Pas River Valley. From a distinct Galego language to a rich apple cider culture, this region has adapted to sometimes challenging conditions.

07902.alsoLocated: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Cape Verde, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, DRC, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Guinea-Bissau, Honduras, Lesser Antilles and Guyana, Mexico, Mozambique, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Puerto Rico, Uruguay, Venezuela
07902.overview: The Canary Islands, a Spanish archipelago of volcanic origin, lie off the coast of northwest Africa. With over 2,000 years of human settlement, the area has been home to a number of Indigenous peoples, often referred to collectively as Guanches. With a year-round mild climate and lush vegetation, the islands have a reputation for delicious cuisine, often featuring sancocho fish stew and fresh tropical fruits. From lounging on beaches to kitesurfing, the Canaries offer an array of outdoor adventures for locals and tourists alike. More recently, fueled by an ongoing diaspora, Canarian communities now exist across the globe from Venezuela to Puerto Rico, spreading island culture and values.

07903.overview: The heart of our Spain region lies in the Iberian Peninsula, framed by the granite peaks and plunging falls of the Pyrenees on the French border in the north and sunny Mediterranean beaches in the south. Waves of invaders throughout history, including Celts and Romans, have fought to establish a presence in this region with varying degrees of success. Muslim rule brought advances in science and education, while the Age of Exploration funneled the world’s wealth into Spain’s coffers. Considering the colonial influence of this region, it is unsurprising that Spanish remains the second-most spoken native language to this day.

08000.overview: Geography contributed to the separate people, language, and nation-state that lie at the heart of our Portugal region. The country of Portugal shares its northern and eastern borders with Spain on the western edge of the Iberian Peninsula. Mountains in the north give way to rolling plains in the south, while the Atlantic to the west and south led to a seafaring tradition that enabled the Portuguese to establish a trading empire that circled the globe.

08001.overview: Rising from the Atlantic Ocean about 900 miles west of mainland Portugal, the Azores are a chain of nine volcanic islands shaped by craters, lakes, and black lava cliffs. Settled by the Portuguese in the 1400s, the islands became an important stopping point for sailors crossing the ocean between Europe, Africa, and the Americas. Life in the Azores was often hard, marked by isolation, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions, but strong family ties, faith, and cooperation helped communities endure. Azoreans are known for their resilience, seafaring traditions, dairy farming, and a culture that blends Portuguese roots with island independence.

08002.overview: Rising from the Atlantic Ocean, Madeira is a rugged island of steep cliffs, green mountains, and mild weather shaped by volcanic forces. Discovered by Portuguese sailors in the 1400s, Madeira quickly became an important stop for explorers sailing for Portugal and beyond. Its people built a strong farming culture, carving terraces into hillsides to grow sugarcane and later grapes for the famous Madeira wine. Over centuries, islanders blended seafaring skills, hard work, and close community ties, creating traditions of music, festivals, and hospitality that still define life on the island today.

08101.overview: Cornwall lies at the southwestern tip of England, with rugged cliffs, sandy beaches, and small fishing villages along the Atlantic coast. For centuries, its people fished the sea, farmed in fertile valleys, and mined tin and copper in the hills. Cornish culture is shaped by its Celtic roots, with a distinct language, folklore, and traditions that survive in music, festivals, and place names. Towns like Truro and Penzance served as local trade centers, linking rural communities to maritime commerce. Even today, tourism and fishing remain central, while historic sites and coastal landscapes reflect Cornwall’s long history of resilience and trade.

08102.overview: Devon and Somerset lie in southwestern England, between the Bristol Channel to the north and the English Channel to the south, with rolling hills, river valleys, rugged coasts, and fertile farmland. Farmers long raised sheep and cattle and grew grains, apples, and cider apples, while fishing villages lined the shores. Cities like Exeter, a Roman-founded center, and Plymouth, home to a major naval dockyard, linked the region to wider trade. Celtic roots, medieval churches, and seafaring traditions remain strong. Dartmoor and Exmoor national parks, tourism, cream teas, and busy summer resorts are still a part of local life.

08103.overview: Northern England stretches from the Pennines to the North Sea and Irish Sea coasts, including cities such as Manchester, Liverpool, and Newcastle upon Tyne. Its coal, iron, and textile industries helped drive the Industrial Revolution, shaping dense urban centers and working-class communities. Farming remains important in upland dales and moorlands. Today about 15 million people live in the region, with diverse populations in major cities shaped by migration from across the UK and beyond. Rural landscapes and historic towns reflect centuries of settlement, trade, and cultural development. Strong regional identities persist through dialects, music, and sport.

08104.overview: Northern Wales and North West England share varied landscapes of mountains, coasts, rivers, and fertile plains. In Northern Wales, Eryri (Snowdonia) rises above farming valleys and former slate towns, while North West England includes the Lake District fells, the western Pennines, and major cities such as Liverpool and Manchester. Medieval castles like Caernarfon Castle reflect conflicts between Welsh princes and English kings. The 1800s brought slate quarrying, cotton mills, ports, and railways. Today, Welsh language traditions, football, music, tourism, and strong regional identities remain important across both areas.

08105.overview: Southeastern England stretches from the Thames Valley to the coasts of Kent, Surrey, East Sussex, West Sussex, and Essex, with rolling hills, fertile farmland, and chalk cliffs facing the English Channel and North Sea. London has shaped politics, finance, and culture for centuries, while smaller towns supported farming, fishing, and markets. Medieval churches, castles, and manor houses reflect a long history of settlement. Busy ports like Dover and Southampton linked the region to trade. Railways and motorways later strengthened commuting and commerce. Today, life ranges from global offices to commuter towns, tourism, and modern logistics.

08106.overview: Yorkshire and the East Midlands stretch across northern and central England, from the Pennine uplands and North York Moors to fertile plains and the River Trent valley. Historic cities such as Leeds, Sheffield, York, Nottingham, Leicester, and Derby grew through wool, steel, lace, hosiery, rail engineering, and trade. Roman roads, canals, and railways tied the regions to national markets, while coal mining shaped many towns. Today diverse communities work in manufacturing, logistics, finance, universities, farming, and services, with football clubs, markets, and county traditions still central to daily life.

08107.overview: The West Midlands sits in central England, where rivers like the Severn, Trent, and Tame cut through low hills and broad plains linking Birmingham, Coventry, and Wolverhampton. Early farming villages fed growing market towns, while skilled metalworkers and weavers built local industries. During the Industrial Revolution, Birmingham became known as the “workshop of the world,” and an extensive canal network carried coal, iron, and finished goods between factories. Churches, guilds, and busy markets shaped daily life. Today the region is a major center for manufacturing, universities, and transport, with diverse communities and dense urban corridors stretching across the Midlands.

08150.overview: This region, located in the Irish Sea between Great Britain and Ireland, is a British crown dependency. Inhabited since at least 6500 BCE, it has absorbed a range of cultural influences, including Gaelic, Norse, Scots, and English. This blend is reflected in the island’s folklore, in which sea gods, fairies, giants, and spirits are said to inhabit its glens and coastline. The island also maintains its own legal and political systems, including its parliament, Tynwald, which has been continuously active for at least 600 years. In addition to its unique history, mythology, and language, the Isle of Man has an active musical tradition rooted in its Celtic and Norse heritage.

08201.overview: Southern Wales stretches from the rocky Bristol Channel coast to green valleys and low mountains shaped by rivers like the Taff and Tawe. For centuries, its people built close-knit communities around farming, fishing, and later coal mining and steelmaking. During the Industrial Revolution, towns such as Cardiff, Swansea, and Merthyr Tydfil grew rapidly as workers labored in mines and factories, making the region one of Britain’s industrial centers. Hard work, strong unions, and shared struggles helped create a deep sense of solidarity. Today, southern Wales blends its working-class history with pride in Welsh language, music, rugby, and a growing cultural life.

08301.overview: The Hebrides and Western Highlands of Scotland are shaped by rugged mountains, deep glens, Atlantic islands, sea lochs, and stormy coasts. For centuries, life in both areas centered on clans, fishing, crofting, cattle raising, and the Gaelic language, which is still spoken in some communities, especially the Outer Hebrides. Clan loyalties influenced local law and warfare until the British government weakened clan power after the failed Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745. During the Highland Clearances, many families were evicted or emigrated overseas. Despite hardship, local culture endures through ceilidh music, storytelling, tartan traditions, and strong ties to land and sea.

08302.overview: North East Scotland and its surrounding isles stretch from rocky North Sea cliffs and rolling farmland to windswept islands like Orkney and Shetland, shaped by strong seas and long winters. The people here have a history rooted in fishing, farming, and seafaring, with deep Norse influence from Viking settlers who left behind place names, traditions, and stone ruins. Medieval castles guarded the coast, while towns such as Aberdeen grew wealthy from trade and later from North Sea oil. Islanders developed close-knit communities, distinct dialects, and traditions of storytelling, music, and craftsmanship that still shape life today.

08305.overview: Ulster, Ireland is known for its rolling hills, rugged coastlines, and historic cities like Belfast and Derry. Once home to powerful Gaelic clans, the region later became central to the Plantation of Ulster in the early 1600s, when Scottish and English settlers arrived. This mix helped shape a unique cultural identity found in dialects, music, and traditions. Traditional Irish tunes played on fiddles and flutes echo through pubs and festivals, while linen weaving recalls an important industrial past. From the Glens of Antrim to Lough Neagh, modern life includes busy cafés, universities, film studios, farming towns, soccer and Gaelic games, and growing tourism.

08310.overview: Located in southern Scotland, the Lowlands and Central Belt combine gentle hills, fertile valleys, and the country’s most densely populated urban corridor. The Central Belt, stretching broadly between Glasgow and Edinburgh, became the heart of heavy industry, commerce, government, and higher education, while surrounding Lowland farmland supplied grain, cattle, and wool to growing markets. Traditional culture combines Scottish heritage with urban influence—seen in poetry, song, and craftsmanship. The Scots language, ceilidh dances, Hogmanay celebrations, and local festivals remain part of community life.

08401.overview: Our Munster region stretches across much of Ireland’s southern and southwestern coasts and is home to cities like Cork, Limerick, and Waterford. Munster is famed for its many castles and early monasteries, including Blarney Castle and the Rock of Cashel, and for its strong traditions in Irish folk music. Many goddesses from Irish mythology—Clíodhna, Áine, and Mór Muman, to name a few—are associated with this region, as are legends like the druid-god Mug Ruith and the high king Brian Boru. Hurling, rugby, and soccer are all popular sports, and local food specialties include fresh seafood, spiced beef, and artisanal cheeses from the region’s villages and seaside towns.

08402.overview: Our Connacht region covers Ireland’s western province, including the counties of Galway, Mayo, Sligo, Leitrim, and Roscommon. Known for its stunning scenery—rugged coastlines, bogs, and mountains like the Twelve Bens and Nephin Beg—the region also has deep Gaelic roots. Irish (Gaeilge) is still spoken in Gaeltacht areas, and ancient sites like tombs and ringforts dot the landscape. Early Christian churches and towers also mark its history. Folklore plays a big role, with legends such as Queen Medb and the Fianna. Today, tourism is important, as visitors explore Connemara National Park, scenic roads, and the vibrant city of Galway.

08403.overview: Our Donegal region lies in the northwest corner of Ireland, in the province of Ulster. It is part of the Republic of Ireland. Known for its high cliffs, rugged mountains, and ancient castles, it is geographically isolated. It is only connected to the rest of Ireland by a small border with County Leitrim. People have lived there since prehistoric times, leaving behind stone circles and ringforts. Medieval monastic ruins are evidence of the later arrival of Christianity. Donegal has a strong Gaelic culture. The Irish name for County Donegal, Dún na nGall, means “fort of the foreigners,” a nod to early Viking or seafaring contact. Traditional music, dancing, and storytelling are still part of everyday life.

08404.overview: Bordered by the Irish Sea and home to the famed rolling hills of Ireland’s landscapes, our Leinster region covers Ireland’s eastern provinces, including the capital city, Dublin. Once home to early Irish kingdoms, Leinster later became the center of English power in Ireland. This history is still visible in the region’s old buildings and Georgian architecture. Leinster is rich in Irish mythology, with legends about Fionn mac Cumhaill, leprechauns, and púcaí—magical creatures that can change shape. Some people still leave a bowl of champ (mashed potatoes with scallions and butter) under a hawthorn tree as an offering to fairies. Today, Leinster remains Ireland’s most populated and economically active region.
